title: Project memory: CLAUDE.md and rules files
subtitle: Write down what the agent cannot guess, keep it short, and review it like code.

c.v: This story is made up, but you may know it.
Sana's team moved their tests from Jest to Vitest last spring. The agent did not know. Every few days it wrote a new test file that imported from
. The tests failed, Sana typed "we use Vitest, not Jest", and the agent fixed it.
The next morning, a new session started. The agent made the same mistake again. Two weeks later, a teammate found the same error in a
. Each person had corrected the agent many times, but the correction lived only in old chat sessions.

blocks.v:
- Tests use Vitest. Import from `vitest`, never from `@jest/globals`.
- Run one file with `pnpm vitest run path/to/file.test.ts`.

c.v: She committed it, and the team reviewed it like any other change. The mistake stopped, for everyone, in every session.

Your corrections, your team's habits and the trap you found last week are gone.
A memory file fixes this. It is a plain Markdown file that the tool loads at the start of every session.
Think of it as the note you would give a new teammate on day one: how to build, how to test, and what not to touch.
Every major tool has one. The names differ:
is a shared format that many tools read. Its site calls it a "README for agents".
A memory file is context, not a law. It makes good behaviour more likely, but it does not force it. Keep it short, so the important lines are not lost, and put hard rules in code.

Where the files live in Claude Code
As of October 2026, Claude Code reads memory files from several places, from broad to specific:
An organization can also install a managed file for every user on a machine. It loads first, before your user file.
At launch, Claude Code loads the files in your working folder and in every folder above it. Files in subfolders load later, when the agent reads, writes or edits a file in that subfolder.
The files are joined together, not replaced. Instructions closer to your working folder are read last.
If two files disagree, the agent may follow either one.
So do not let them conflict.

Memory files are an attack path
The agent reads memory files as trusted instructions. That makes them a target. OWASP describes
as an attack where a model "accepts input from external sources, such as websites or files".
In March 2025, Pillar Security showed an attack on

. They called it the "Rules File Backdoor". They hid instructions in the file using invisible Unicode characters, such as zero-width joiners. In their demo, a Cursor agent asked for a simple HTML page added a script from an attacker's site, and did not mention it.
The researchers say the hidden characters also stayed invisible in GitHub pull request reviews at the time. In May 2025, GitHub added a warning for files with hidden Unicode text.
In an interactive session, Claude Code shows a trust dialog when you start it in a folder you have not trusted before.
It also asks before it loads imports that point outside the project, to protect you from files other people commit.
These help, but they do not replace reading the files yourself.

q.v: Why does a coding agent need a project memory file?

options.v: Because the model forgets the programming language between sessions.
Because each session starts with a fresh context, without your team's commands and conventions.
Because the file makes the model run faster.

why.v: Claude Code's docs say each session begins with a fresh context window. The memory file brings your team's context back every time.

q.v: Which line belongs in a project CLAUDE.md?

options.v: The production database password, so the agent can run migrations.
for fast tests. The full suite needs Docker."

why.v: Commands the agent cannot guess belong in the file. Secrets never do, and long docs should be linked, not copied.

q.v: . Which CLAUDE.md files load at launch?

options.v: The ones in that folder and every folder above it, plus your user file. Files in deeper subfolders load later, when the agent works there.
Every CLAUDE.md in the whole repository, at once.

why.v: Claude Code loads files from the working directory and the folders above it at launch. Subfolder files load on demand.

q.v: The agent must never edit files in

options.v: In CLAUDE.md, written in capital letters.
In a hook or permission rule that blocks the edit, with a short note in CLAUDE.md that explains why.

why.v: Memory files are context, not enforced configuration. A hook or a deny rule is code that runs every time.

q.v: You clone an unknown open-source repo and run an agent in it. What is the main risk from its rules files?

options.v: They may slow the agent down.
They may contain hidden instructions that change what the agent does, which is a form of prompt injection.
They may use the wrong Markdown style.

why.v: The agent reads these files as instructions. OWASP calls content from files that changes a model's behaviour indirect prompt injection.
